title: Verdant Labs — Usage Lighthouse: Console attribution workshop
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood Console: per-route usage lenses, cost allocation, anomaly detection, and export hooks. Discussed Verdant's current self-hosted stack, FinOps needs, and next steps for a pilot + security docs.
next_steps: Jordan to share console export sample and route-tagging guide by 2026-10-04
Morgan to run a short throughput/latency benchmark with Verdant test payloads (target week of 2026-10-11)
Send SOC2 and architecture whitepaper to Verdant (Jordan) by 2026-10-02
Schedule pilot kickoff (30-day pilot) — aim for 2026-10-18
action_items: Jordan - send pricing tiers + example billing export (due 2026-10-04)
Morgan - prepare benchmark plan and sample script (due 2026-10-08)
Priya - share representative 12-hour trace and a small prompt set for quality checks (due 2026-10-06)
Marisol - confirm internal billing owner and desired chargeback dimensions (due 2026-10-05)
transcript:
Header: Verdant Labs — Usage Lighthouse console workshop
Date: 2026-09-30
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Morgan Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Verdant Head of ML), Ethan Cole (Verdant Infra), Marisol Ruiz (Verdant FinOps)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Priya: Yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:08] Jordan: Cool. Quick agenda — I'll do a high level on what the Console provides for usage and cost attribution, Morgan will jump into the per-route dashboards and a small walkthrough, then we'll do Q&A and next steps. Does that sound good?
[00:18] Marisol: Yeah that works. We're mainly focused on being able to bill product teams and to surface cost spikes.
[00:22] Ethan: And we have a couple of infra constraints — we run a hybrid k8s cluster on-prem + cloud, traffic bursts at 9am and 4pm PST, and we need predictable tail latency.
[00:33] Morgan: Understood. We'll show the route split and tail-latency lenses. Also show how caching and batching impacts token-level cost.

[02:05] Jordan: Quick qualify — Priya, could you remind us of your current model stack and how you tag requests today?
[02:12] Priya: Sure, so we're serving two families — an instruction-tuned 7B open model for general assistant and a smaller reranker for search. We use an ingress gateway that tags requests with product:search or product:assist, but it's pretty minimal — sometimes product teams don't set tags consistently.
[02:30] Ethan: We also have a central billing where we take raw infra spend and try to apportion via a homegrown script, but it never matches per-route consumption because of batching and shared caches.
[02:42] Morgan: That's very common — Redwood's console does route-level attribution using request metadata and token accounting, and it factors in batching and KV prefix caches so your per-route unit cost is more accurate.

[04:10] Jordan: Ok let's jump into the Console. I'm going to share my screen — I have a demo tenant with synthetic traffic mapped to Verdant's route names.
[04:18] [screen share starts]
[04:22] Morgan: On the left is Usage -> Routes. You'll see each route which we can tag by product, team, SLA tier, et cetera. The main table shows total tokens, avg latency p50/p95/p99, and an estimated cost column.
[04:40] Priya: That estimated cost — is that including batching efficiency and GPU-time amortization?
[04:47] Morgan: Yes, it's our cost model. We use per-token compute seconds plus a batching factor. There's an internal model for amortizing kernel warmup and KV cache hits. It's an estimate but we've found it tracks within about 7-12% versus actual runbooks depending on workload.
[05:05] Ethan: Does it support custom prices? We have negotiated reserved capacity rates with cloud provider.
[05:10] Jordan: Yep — you can set custom per-model and per-hardware cost overrides at account level, so your chargeback matches internal rates.

[06:00] [06:00] Morgan: Here's the route detail drilldown for product:search. You can see token distribution over time, a breakdown by user segment, and an annotations lane where we surface anomalies — spikes in tokens or sudden p99 shifts.
[06:23] Marisol: That anomaly detection — is it rule-based or ML-driven?
[06:27] Morgan: It's hybrid — baseline is time-series with seasonal adjustment and we add heuristics for token-burst detection. You can tune sensitivity.

[07:50] Priya: I see a "prefix cache hits" column — how are we measuring that? Our engineers worried that the KV cache is shared and sometimes gets stale.
[08:00] Morgan: Good question. We instrument prefix/KV hits per request. For on-prem we can also surface cache eviction metrics. Staleness is out of band — you'd need a TTL or invalidation signal from your app, but we show hit rates and the effective token savings.

[09:30] [09:30] Jordan: Walk us through an export. Marisol, you mentioned you want a CSV that ties back to accounting?
[09:36] Marisol: Correct. We want route, team, token count, estimated cost, and a reference to the raw request IDs for auditing.
[09:44] Morgan: We have a scheduled export feature — it can push to S3 or a secure FTP with per-day or per-hour slices. It includes route tags, model id, hardware class, token counts, and both estimated and raw compute seconds. We can add a reference field that links to trace IDs.
[10:03] Ethan: Nice. Can we also get a mapping to service names so our billing pipeline can join? We use service_id in BigQuery.
[10:09] Morgan: You can map a Redwood route to your internal service_id; we support custom metadata fields.

[12:12] Priya: On the security front — we need audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration. Where are audit logs kept for private deployments?
[12:20] Jordan: For Redwood Private we ship logs to your S3 or logging cluster. Audit trails include request headers, model version, routing decisions, and operator actions. We also integrate with AWS KMS and common HSM providers for key management.
[12:35] Marisol: And SAML?
[12:38] Morgan: SAML and SCIM for provisioning, RBAC for the console with role templates. For SOC2 docs Jordan will share the compliance packet.

[14:50] [14:50] Morgan: Now a quick demo of a cost-playbook: imagine product:assist spikes daily at 9am due to a batch job. We can create an alert that watches per-route token rate and p95 latency and then trigger an automated route policy — fallback to a cheaper quantized variant, or limit burst capacity, or divert to a reserved pool.
[15:16] Priya: We need to be careful about that, quality can regress if we fallback automatically. Is there a canary or A/B?
[15:23] Morgan: Yes we support gradual rollouts and can specify quality gates using evaluation sets. If quality metrics degrade beyond threshold the policy rolls back.

[17:40] Ethan: A specific infra question — we have GPU nodes that are shared across teams, how does Redwood attribute GPU time when multiple routes are multiplexed?
[17:49] Morgan: Attribution is token-first. We track tokens at request boundaries and account for batching windows. For concurrent multiplexing we estimate per-request compute seconds by dividing batch compute by token share and factoring in manifest kernel usage. It's approximate but better than flat allocation.

[19:55] Marisol: Can the Console surface chargebacks by business unit and by cost-center tags?
[20:02] Morgan: Absolutely — you can group routes by arbitrary tags and the UI has pivoting. We also have a chargeback export that creates ledger-ready rows (date, route, cost-center, tokens, cost).

[22:30] [22:30] Priya: How would a 30-day pilot look operationally? We want to validate per-route costs and run a small benchmark for latency and throughput.
[22:37] Jordan: Typical pilot is: 1) onboarding and route tagging (~3 days), 2) mirror or sampled traffic for 2 weeks to compare attribution vs your existing script, and 3) a short benchmark with representative prompts for throughput/latency characterization. Morgan will run the benchmark and produce a report.

[24:10] Morgan: I'll sketch the benchmark plan now — we'll need a representative prompt corpus (Priya to provide), a 12-hour trace to simulate diurnal patterns, and a target SLA for p95. We'll run both hosted Redwood and a Dedicated config to compare.
[24:30] Priya: Ok I can extract a 12-hour trace and a ~200 prompt eval set.

[26:02] [26:02] Jordan: Quick pricing note — our hosted product bills per token and has tiered discounts. Dedicated is a reserved capacity model with monthly commit. We can model both in the Console so you see estimated monthly run-rate.
[26:22] Marisol: We're leaning towards reserved for stable traffic but want to validate the numbers first.

[28:00] Morgan: Back to the UI — here's an example of a cost-variance dashboard. It shows forecast vs actual spend and highlights routes with >15% variance month-over-month. You can click a route and see the raw trace and even replay the request in a sandbox to inspect outputs.
[28:27] Priya: Replaying requests — is that safe for PII?
[28:32] Morgan: For replay we mask sensitive fields by default and you can disable replay on certain routes. Also for Private deployments the replay data stays in your VPC, never leaves the customer boundary.

[30:40] Ethan: A small nit — we've had issues mapping SDK-level request IDs back to our logs. Can we add a per-request correlation id?
[30:48] Jordan: Yes you can pass an x-correlation-id header and Redwood surfaces it in traces and exports.

[32:10] [32:10] Priya: Are there any gotchas with quantized model variants? We worry about hallucination increases.
[32:18] Morgan: Quantized variants reduce compute but sometimes micro-degrade quality. The Console's Optimize recommendations will suggest which routes are safe to quantize based on evals and win/loss delta. You'll get a predicted quality impact and you can guard with A/B testing.

[34:50] Marisol: Competitors we looked at weren't giving us per-route token accounting — mostly they report per-endpoint spend. That mismatch is what breaks our chargebacks.
[34:58] Jordan: Right, route-level attribution is specific to request metadata and token accounting; endpoints are coarser.

[36:05] [36:05] Priya: On private deployment — do we get the same Console features?
[36:10] Morgan: Yes. Private can run the control plane in your VPC and the observability/telemetry can point to your backend. There are some capsule features like autoscaling adapters that require a small agent but it's standard.

[38:20] Ethan: Any latency overhead from collection? We care about added p50.
[38:26] Morgan: Collection is asynchronous — tracing adds negligible overhead. The only latency hit would be if you enabled synchronous enrichment (we generally avoid that for low latency routes).

[40:00] Jordan: Let's capture the key open questions — 1) Priya to share prompt set and trace; 2) Marisol to confirm billing owner; 3) Morgan to run benchmark; 4) Jordan to send SOC2 and pricing.

[41:15] Priya: One more thought — can we define SLA tiers per route so we can automatically route premium customers to higher tier models during congestion?
[41:24] Morgan: Yes that's part of smart routing; you can define policy trees based on route tags and SLA.

[43:40] Marisol: On the export we want daily granularity and we want the per-row CSV to include both estimated and realized compute secs plus an explanation column for delta (e.g., batching efficiency).
[43:51] Morgan: We can include a computed delta column and an export that contains both values.

[46:05] [46:05] Jordan: Ok we're coming up on time. Any final questions?
[46:12] Ethan: Will the pilot require opening ports or special firewall rules?
[46:16] Morgan: For on-prem agents we need outbound to Redwood control plane on a couple of IPs, or you can run a fully air-gapped variant with a one-time swap of artifacts. We'll share docs.
[46:30] Priya: And data residency — we need EU-only storage for some routes. Is that supported?
[46:36] Jordan: Yup, you can pin routes/models to regions or private deployment zones for residency.

[49:00] [49:00] Marisol: Last logistical — timeline for docs?
[49:05] Jordan: I'll attach SOC2, architecture whitepaper, and a sample billing export by 2026-10-02.

[50:40] Priya: Thanks everyone this was useful.
[50:44] Jordan: Thanks for the time. We'll follow up with the pilot plan and next steps.
[50:50] [call ends]

Notes about transcript: occasional ASR artifacts present — e.g., "K V cache" appears split, "Redwood Opti-mize" is sometimes mis-typed, speaker overlap at 15:24.
